title: Budget 101: where Australia's tax revenue comes from and where it goes
summary: A ready-made picture of the revenue and spending mix, and of how bracket creep props up the budget, for any fiscal policy answer.
lede: Guardian economics correspondent Patrick Commins explains the federal tax mix and spending mix ahead of the March 2025 budget, noting that a decade of deficits is forecast. Using PBO data, he shows income tax's share of revenue could climb towards 46% by the mid-2030s if bracket creep returned.

Share of tax from individuals' income tax
Share of tax from company income tax
Individuals' income tax share if bracket creep returned
Social security and welfare share of spending
Interest on national debt, share of spending
2024-25 deficit

terms.def: Rising incomes push people into higher tax brackets, so average tax rates rise when thresholds are not indexed.
The proportions of total revenue raised from different taxes.
Government spending is greater than revenue in a financial year.

angle: Use the revenue and spending splits to describe the composition of the budget, then link bracket creep to the progressive tax system and to how deficits are reduced.

questions.q: Outline what is meant by 'bracket creep'.
Explain how bracket creep affects the budget outcome and the distribution of income.

Secondary source (newspaper explainer using PBO charts); pie chart percentages differ slightly from the text, and some chart values were not legible, so figures here are taken from the text. Newspaper article reproduced for classroom use.

title: Budget to reveal tax burden at its lowest since the pandemic
summary: Shows the budget's tax-to-GDP ratio, the political fight over fiscal guardrails, and why a return to deficit limits new spending.
lede: SMH reports that the 2025-26 budget will show tax falling to 23.1% of GDP, while the budget heads back into deficit after two years of surplus. The Coalition attacks the scale of spending, and the government points to savings and a $1.8 billion energy bill relief extension.

Spending exceeds revenue in a financial year.

questions.q: Explain one limitation of fiscal policy in the current economy, using the article.

title: Home-building productivity has halved since 1995, Productivity Commission finds
summary: Concrete productivity and housing-supply data for microeconomic reform answers: why supply side policy matters for affordability.
lede: SMH reports Productivity Commission research finding Australia builds half as many homes per hour worked as in 1995. Build times have lengthened sharply, and the Commission urges an independent review of building regulation.

angle: Link slow building productivity to a leftward-shifted short-run supply and to the case for microeconomic reform (regulation, licensing, skills).

questions.q: Explain how microeconomic reform could raise productivity in home building.

title: Gittins: ACCC report shows supermarkets are overcharging
summary: A market power and cost-push inflation case study: oligopoly pricing power against the conventional demand-pull explanation.
lede: Ross Gittins argues the ACCC supermarkets report shows Coles and Woolworths hold market power and raised margins over five years. He contends economists and the RBA have overlooked oligopoly as a source of cost-push inflation.

figures.label: Coles and Woolworths share of supermarket sales

terms.def: A market dominated by a few large firms.

Government rules that promote competition and limit abuse of market power.

questions.q: Distinguish between demand-pull and cost-push inflation, using the supermarket example.

note: Older item (published Mar 2025): figures are as at that date; check for newer data before quoting. Opinion column (Ross Gittins); the ACCC findings are quoted second-hand, check the ACCC report before quoting. Newspaper article reproduced for classroom use.

title: Deloitte Access Economics: Labor's second term needs a bolder reform agenda
summary: An economist's assessment of the policy agenda after the 2025 election: near-term cost-of-living policy versus structural reform on tax, productivity and the budget.
lede: Deloitte Access Economics partners say Labor's election win gives it a strong platform but that its agenda lacks ambition. They warn of deficits as far as the eye can see and an outsized tax burden for younger generations without reform.

lede: The ABS reported GDP growth of just 0.2% in the March quarter, below forecasts, with equipment investment, foreign student spending and state infrastructure all falling. Annual growth held at 1.3% and GDP per capita fell for the ninth time in 11 quarters.
